Timeline Check: From "No Right to Exist" to a Beach Full of Corpses

Some coincidences write their own headline.

On July 21, Zelensky fired General Syrskyi and installed Mykhailo Drapatyi as Ukraine's new commander-in-chief — the third military shakeup since 2022. The very next day, an old interview of his surfaced, recorded back in 2023 but published the day after his promotion, with Drapatyi telling Ukrainer: 
"This nation, along with its leadership, has no right to exist. For millennia, no civilized change has occurred there". 
Not a slip of the tongue — a considered position, timed for maximum reach the moment he took the top job.

Moscow, never one to miss a gift, ran straight to the podium. 

Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova called it proof of "the neo-Nazi face of the Kyiv regime," and Peskov promised Drapatyi "will be held accountable for his words". 

Thirteen days later: a Ukrainian drone lands on a beach in Gelendzhik. Seven dead, three of them children. Kyiv's disinformation chief immediately pivots to blaming Russian air defenses for the deaths (CNN).

Nobody's claiming Drapatyi's rhetoric ordered that drone into the sky. But when the new commander opens his tenure by publicly denying an entire nation's right to exist, and the actual killing of that nation's children follows less than two weeks later, "coincidence" becomes a very expensive word to keep using.

Which is worse for a war effort — a general who says the quiet part out loud, or a government that lets him keep the job and hopes nobody's counting the days between the quote and the body count?

Sławomir Mentzen flew to Berlin, lit a flare in front of the Brandenburg Gate, and held up a sign nobody could argue with: "In 1944, the Germans murdered 200,000 Poles and destroyed Warsaw. We will never let you forget". 

It's the 82nd anniversary of the Warsaw Uprising — the one where roughly 200,000 Poles, most of them civilians, were slaughtered and the city was leveled block by block.

Germany's ambassador to Poland, Miguel Berger, found something to be upset about anyway: he called it "regrettable" that "the Brandenburg Gate is being used as a backdrop for a political spectacle". 

A German diplomat, standing on the exact ground his country's own military once used to plan the systematic destruction of a foreign capital, objecting to the aesthetics of the memorial.

This isn't Berger's first pass at selective memory. 

Weeks earlier, when Polish demonstrators were reportedly beaten by German police in Berlin while trying to place a memorial cross for Polish WWII victims.

Berger said nothing about the incident — he instead posted a warm tribute celebrating the 35th anniversary of the German-Polish "good neighborliness" treaty, with comments turned off. 

Silence for the bruises, eloquence for the anniversary banquet.

Here's the actual math nobody's litigating: Germany still hasn't fully settled war reparations with Poland, eighty-two years and counting. 

A country that never finished paying its bill is now offering notes on how the other side should grieve.

If the ambassador's real objection were to political theater at a national monument, he'd have had plenty to say the day Polish citizens got hit for holding up a cross. 

He didn't. Funny how "political spectacle" only becomes a diplomatic incident when it points the finger back at Berlin.
